title: You Didn’t Lose Everything… You Were Being Positioned
paragraphs:
You Didn’t Lose Everything… You Were Being Positioned
The Pattern of Losing Everything Before Purpose — Why God Empties What He Intends to Fill
There’s a kind of silence that only comes after everything falls apart.

Not the peaceful kind. Not the quiet of rest. I’m talking about the silence that follows unanswered prayers… the kind that echoes in an empty room after something—or someone—you loved is suddenly gone. The kind where your faith feels like it’s standing in ruins, looking around, asking God questions you’re almost afraid to say out loud.
You called it loss.
He calls it preparation.

Because if you trace the fingerprints of God through Scripture—if you really look closely, beyond the polished sermons and surface-level encouragement—you’ll start to see a pattern that feels almost uncomfortable to admit:
God often allows people to lose everything… right before He gives them everything they were actually created for.
And that truth doesn’t feel good when you’re living it.

It didn’t feel good for Joseph when his own brothers stripped him of his coat, his identity, and threw him into a pit like he meant nothing. The Hebrew word used in Genesis 37:24 for “pit” is בּוֹר (bor), a cistern—empty, dark, abandoned. No water. No life. Just isolation. Joseph didn’t know that the pit wasn’t his grave—it was God’s doorway.

It didn’t feel good for Job when everything collapsed in a single breath. His children gone. His wealth gone. His health gone. And yet in Job 1:21, he whispers something that still shakes heaven and earth:

“יְהוָה נָתַן וַיהוָה לָקָח; יְהִי שֵׁם יְהוָה מְבֹרָךְ”
“The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD.”
Who says that… unless they’ve reached a place where God is no longer a transaction—but everything?

It didn’t feel good for Peter when he denied Jesus three times and heard the rooster crow. The Greek word in Luke 22:62 says he wept bitterly—ἔκλαυσεν πικρῶς (eklausen pikrōs). That wasn’t a quiet tear. That was a soul breaking under the weight of failure. That was the kind of crying that makes you question if you’ll ever be the same again.
And yet… that same broken Peter becomes the rock the early Church stands on.
Do you see it yet?
The pattern is not punishment.
It’s positioning.
Because God cannot pour purpose into hands that are still clinging to what will destroy you.
So sometimes… He lets it fall apart.
Not because He’s absent.
But because He’s intentional.
In John 12:24, Jesus Himself reveals this pattern with a statement that sounds almost like a warning:
“ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν, ἐὰν μὴ ὁ κόκκος τοῦ σίτου… ἀποθάνῃ, αὐτὸς μόνος μένει· ἐὰν δὲ ἀποθάνῃ, πολὺν καρπὸν φέρει.”
“Truly, truly I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.”
Read that again.
If it doesn’t die… it stays alone.
There are things in your life that had to die… not because they were worthless, but because they were seeds, not the harvest.
And seeds don’t look like purpose.
They look like loss.

That relationship you thought would last forever. That job you built your identity around. That version of your life you planned so carefully. When it fell apart, it didn’t feel like planting—it felt like burial.
But heaven saw it differently.
Heaven saw planting.
Because God is not in the business of taking from you just to leave you empty. He is in the business of emptying you so He can fill you with something eternal.
And if you’re honest… some of what you lost was quietly killing who you were called to become.
We don’t like saying that part.
We don’t like admitting that sometimes the very things we begged God to protect… were the things blocking His purpose.
So He let them go.
And it hurt.
Deeply.
But purpose is not born in comfort.
Purpose is born in surrender.
The kind where you finally stop asking, “Why did I lose this?” and start asking, “God, what are You building now?”
Because He is always building.
Even in silence.
Even in absence.
Even when it feels like He walked away.

Isaiah 61:3 says He gives “beauty for ashes.” The Hebrew word for beauty is פְּאֵר (pe’er), meaning a headdress, a crown. Think about that—God doesn’t just replace your ashes. He crowns you with what comes from them.
Ashes are what’s left after something has been completely consumed.
So if you’re holding ashes right now… you’re closer to a crown than you think.
But here’s the part nobody tells you plainly:
You cannot carry both.
You cannot hold onto the ashes and receive the crown.
At some point, you have to let go.
Fully.
Not halfway. Not conditionally.
Fully.
That’s where transformation happens.
That’s where Jesus meets you—not in the version of you that has it all together, but in the version that finally admits it doesn’t.
Because the Gospel itself is the ultimate pattern of losing everything before purpose.
Jesus lost His reputation… His followers… His freedom… His body… His life.
On the cross, He cried out in Aramaic:

“אֵלִי אֵלִי לְמָה שְׁבַקְתַּנִי”
“Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani?”
“My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?” (Matthew 27:46)
That wasn’t weakness.
That was the weight of redemption.
Because three days later… purpose exploded out of what looked like total loss.
The resurrection didn’t erase the crucifixion.
It fulfilled it.
And that means your losses are not the end of your story.
They are the setup.

So if you’re in that place right now—the place where it feels like everything has slipped through your hands… the place where you’re tired of pretending you’re okay… the place where your faith feels more fragile than strong—
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
Let someone see you. Let someone stand with you. You are not alone in this.
And if this spoke directly into your life, don’t keep it to yourself. This could be the moment that pulls them back from the edge.
You’re going to need to read it again on a day when the silence feels louder than your faith.
And if you’re ready to go deeper—really deeper—there’s something for you.
This isn’t surface-level faith. This is transformation.
If you feel God stirring something in you right now… don’t ignore it.
Supporting this mission isn’t just about content—it’s about spreading the Gospel, reaching the broken, and making sure more people encounter the truth that can save their lives.
If you want to be part of that… if you want your life to glorify God not just in words but in action—
Step in.
Because sometimes the most powerful thing you can do after losing everything… is decide who you’re becoming next in Christ.
And maybe… just maybe… what you thought was the end was God refusing to let you settle for less than your calling.
You didn’t lose everything.
You were being positioned.
And the God who emptied your hands is the same God preparing to fill your life with something you never could have imagined.
You just have to trust Him long enough to see it.
What if the breaking wasn’t destruction… but introduction?
